title: Count Ways to Group Overlapping Ranges
statement:
Each entry `ranges[i] = [start_i, end_i]` stands for every integer from `start_i` through `end_i`, endpoints included. Two ranges overlap when some integer lies in both of them (so `[1, 3]` and `[3, 6]` overlap, while `[1, 3]` and `[4, 6]` do not).

Assign every range to one of two groups, either of which may end up empty, so that overlapping ranges always land in the same group. Return how many different assignments are possible, modulo `10^9 + 7`.
notes:
## Intuition

Overlap links ranges into clusters: if `A` overlaps `B` and `B` overlaps `C`, all three must share a group. Each cluster then picks one of the two groups on its own, so with `k` clusters the answer is `2^k`. A brute force could compare every pair and count connected components in O(n²); sorting by start finds the clusters in one sweep, exactly like merging intervals.

## Approach

1. Sort `ranges` by start.
2. Keep `reach`, the largest end seen so far in the current cluster, starting below every possible start.
3. For each range, if `start > reach`, nothing earlier touches it, so it opens a new cluster: double `ways` modulo `MOD`.
4. Extend `reach` to `max(reach, end)`.
5. Return `ways`.

## Example 1, step by step

Example 1 sorted is `[[5, 15], [6, 10]]`. `[5, 15]`: `5 > -1`, so `ways = 2` and `reach = 15`. `[6, 10]`: `6 <= 15`, so it joins the same cluster and `reach` stays `15`. The answer is `2`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n log n) for the sort; the sweep is O(n).
- Space: O(1) beyond the sort.

## Pitfalls

- Shared endpoints count: `[1, 3]` and `[3, 6]` overlap, so the test is `start > reach`, not `>=`.
- Use the running maximum end, not the previous range's end: a long range like `[1, 100]` can cover several later ones.
- `2^k` overflows quickly; reduce modulo `10^9 + 7` after every doubling.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `MOD` | the modulus `10^9 + 7` |
| `ways` | `2` raised to the number of clusters found so far, modulo `MOD` |
| `reach` | the furthest end covered by the current cluster |
| `start`, `end` | the endpoints of the range being examined |

narration.3: Sort by start so overlapping ranges become neighbours in the sweep.
narration.4: Before any cluster is found there is exactly one (empty) assignment.
narration.5: No range has been seen yet, so the covered region ends below 0.
narration.6: Sweep the ranges in order of their start.
narration.7: Does this range begin after everything covered so far?
narration.8: Yes: it starts a new independent cluster, which doubles the number of assignments.
narration.10: Stretch the covered region to include this range's end.
narration.12: Each cluster chose one of two groups independently; return the count.
